legb...@my-dejanews.com wrote:
> I'd like to enthusiastically endorse Michael Beer's proposal for making First
> Strike resolve first, before Strike:Combat ends. This seems to me to be the
> kind of fix we SHOULD be making, instead of altering explicit card text. I'm
> sure Michael is right to say that it will finally make the Assamites SCARY,
> which is what they should be, and generally to make combat decks better
> against combat- avoidance decks [which in any case will still have Obedience
> and Elysium: the Arboretum].

It's only a "fix" if something is broken (unbalanced or not functioning as
intended). And that doesn't seem to be the case. Assamites have Psyche!,
Hidden Lurker and (to a lesser extent) Rapid Thought to help them deal
with S:CE.

> Now, no-one can acccuse me of being an indiscriminate banner and fixer, and i

> don't intend to start being one now. So i have a proposal for the rules team.
> If we [Michael and I] can prove, from JOL statistics, that the assamites as a
> clan, and celerity as a discipline, are significantly underpowered with
> respect to other clans and disciplines, will you at least consider making the
> change?

Unlikely, since "proving" that a whole clan/discipline is underpowered is
much more difficult than "proving" a card is underpowered. And even so,
proving that a clan is underpowered doesn't prove that the order of strike
resolution is unbalancing.

(Hasn't someone already "proven", from JOL statistics, that one or two of
the clans wins disproportionately? Would you also argue then some change
to the basic rules of the game to impeed them?)

Also, being underpowered is not one of the criteria for errata:
see Concealed Weapon and a host of Locations from Dark Sovereigns.

A better plan of attack would be to show that Strike: Combat Ends (and/or
Dodge) is overpowered when allowed to resolve before First Strike and that
reversing the order doesn't unbalance the situation in the other direction
(that is, doesn't make First Strike overpowered). Particular attention
should be paid to Muddled Vampire Hunter, since he would be much better
if the strike order were changed, and he's alreay pretty good.

This is something I've already looked at and found no cause to alter the
order of strike resolution from the original design. S:CE can be annoying,
certainly, but it doesn't seem to be overpowered. But you are free to try
your hand at showing otherwise, of course.

My main argument in favor of bumping the priority on First Strike is that there
are too many counters against First Strike versus how difficult it actually is to
get First Strike into play. Consider that Dodge beats it (and is a skilless card,
not to mention all the other dodges in the game), S:CE beats it (and is commonly
available to any clan with Presence, which is available to 4 clans and is one of
the most common skills for a vampire), Fortitude also beats it handily (in the
case of the Muddled Vampire Hunter), and to get a MVH into play still requires an
action that can be blocked and even the D action of the MVH can be blocked without
intercept.

Also, the First Strike celerity attack is conditional and many First-Strike
attacks don't do damage, but rather destroy/steal equipment - again, very
conditional. Why even bother having First Strike if it is so difficult to play
with and currently, the only "tourney worthy" First Strike card is the MVH and he
is really not as good a card as Majesty is, in my opinion.

All I ask is, have you playtested the game with the rules changed to see if it
becomes more balanced? I have playtested retty thoroughly with my group - a group
that makes heavy use of S:CE - and have found that S:CE still maintains its
effectiveness and that First Strike is actually a playable defense now rather than
a "oh man do I wish I played Potence for Immortal Grapple INSTEAD" type of
strategy.

>

Personally, I would endorse the change if and only if you could show
that combat as an entire strategy is too weak and that the "deficiency"
of first strike is a large factor in this. This of course, under 7/7
rulings. I'm pretty sure you cannot do this for a couple of reasons.

a) 7/7 have not been around long enough. Non-JOL non-tournament
anecdotes are all fine and good, but the closest thing we have to a
level, skill-based playing field is JOL, with tournaments coming
second. There has not, however, been enough data from these sources to
show all that much. And, since combat decks are improved under 7/7 (at
least IMO), there could be a large difference.

b) Combat decks are, in fact, not that weak. You can say that a certain
clan is weak, or a discipline is weak (celerity isn't), but that's not
really any concern of the rules team. As long as one clan or discipline
doesn't completely dominate all others (no pun intended, but now that I
notice, it's a good pun...), that's a problem for deck-builders not
rules-makers. You're never forced to make a one-clan deck, so Assamites
compared to Ventrue or whatever isn't a valid comparison. Combat versus
bleed is an okay comparison, and here I don't think that combat is
really inferior, and if it is, I doubt making meaningless changes to
first strike rules will really change that.

In fact, I tend to feel that one-clan decks are harmful to the game, and
one-discipline decks nearly so. So, any whining about the inability to
make decks for a clan (e.g. City Gangrel) will be met with my unbridled
opposition. It seems to me to be akin to whining that Well-Aimed Car is
just too weak to build a deck around and arguing that it should be
changed to be usable first round and/or at close range.

As I said somewhere else, Fast Reactions and Hidden Lurker emulate an
attack that the opposing minion is not aware of. As long as he is aware
of an attack, he may not be able to hit you before you smack him, but he
may be able to avoid your fist. A vamp with celerity is faster than a
vamp without it, but celerity (or even First Strike spelled out) doesn't
give you surprise. It simply means you can strike a bit faster (and
celerity allows you to strike *more* if you play the right cards). If

Actually, Majesty never has to be turned on. It is in fact always on.
The reasons that it is not a permanent card are: a) Game balance - that
would be nasty powerful, b) Possession of the discipline - not all
vampires with presence would normally have access to Majesty, it is a
5th level discipline (the highest most vampires can ever get). Since
there are only 2 levels of a discipline in the game, and a card can be
played with either level, this is somewhat simulated by the requirement
of having the card in hand when needed, c) Not infallible - while
automatic, Majesty is not infallible. A vampire would normally be able
to make a willpower(I think) roll to avoid the effects. Since your
crypt cards don't have the necessary stats on them, this is simulated to
a point by the fact that another Majesty card must be used each time the
Majestic vampire "uses" the ability.

playing for ante. One example: My opponent and I each had about 5 pool
left and were pretty even in terms of minions. I had anted a Body
Flare, while he anted a Surprise Influence. My deck used protean, but I
had no need for Surprise Influence, as my deck had the best political
power in the league. He, on the other hand, sorely needed that SI for
vote protection but didn't use protean. So, I offered to withdraw, if
he would let me. He pondered for a bit. I warned him, "If you do not

losing..." Since the game was even and neither one of us was sure of a
victory, he agreed. We then agreed to discard each turn until one of us
had a depleted library and then that person would withdraw. We didn't
actually play out the rest of the game, but agreed that I had withdrawn

Yes. The effective Potence pure-rush combat deck that uses Immortal
Grapples and close-range combat does not usually want to throw in Gates or
Lids, even if they could sometimes be useful. A Flash to make the rest
of your deck work the way it's supposed to is usually much better.

A Malkavian deck (stealth and bleed or whatever) usually has much more
flexibility in putting in 'prayer' cards like Muddled Vampire Hunter
than a pure-rush combat deck does in putting in 'prayer' cards like
Computer Hacking, Inveraray Scotland, Laptop Computer, Thrown Sewer
Lid, etc. This is because the pure-rush combat deck relies on relatively
large multi-card combos to be effective. Things that can't be played
in those combos under normal circumstances tend to cause crippling hand
jams and can severely reduce the effectiveness of the deck.

Any kind of non-combat deck can usually much better afford to have a
few 'prayer' cards that are only *really* useful under certain conditions,
because the main focus of the deck doesn't revolve around large combos
with intensive card cycling. That's why Muddled Vampire Hunter is more
playable to a Malk stealth-bleed deck than Thrown Sewer Lid is to
an Immortal Grapple pure-rush combat deck.

Mike Bohlman wrote:
"No, Drawing Out the Beast is much better. It counters weapons and any combat
defense that depends on maneuvers to get away from your hands. The +1 hand
damage the other vampire gets only comes into play if you are facing another
heavy hitter. In that case, they want to be at close range anyway."

While a very good point, building a Pot/Ani deck is much harder than building
the Pot/Obf deck, due to the vampire selection. A Pot/Obf deck has at its
disposal (not counting the single discipline Pot vamps like KoKo and Hasina):

Duck (3) pot, obf
Agatha (4) POT, obf
Agripina (4) pot, OBF
Sammy (4) pot, obf
Olivia (5) POT, OBF
Nigel (5) POT, obf

and half of those have POT to boot. The Pot/Ani vamps available close to the
same cost are are:

Raziya (3) pot, ani
Sammy (4) pot, ani
Shane (4) pot, ani
Tiberius (5) pot, ani
Grendel (5) pot, ani
Nigel (5) POT, ANI

Of these, only Nigel has POT (which is _very_ important to the Rush deck, far
more than either OBF or ANI), and paying 5 points for either Tiberius or
Grendel in a Pot/Ani Rush deck is a real waste.

Not to say that Pot/Ani isn't a really good combat combination, but to make a
good Pot/Ani deck, you need bigger (and consequently slower) vampires, and you
really should throw Song of Serenity into the mix to break even with the DotB
damage.

That *is* a heavy devotion to one card. In my pot/cel pure-rush combat
decks, there is a great reliance on a few of the most effective cards:
Immortal Grapple, Torn Signpost, Bum's Rush, etc. In a 90-card pure-rush

like Ambush quite a bit too, although Peter doesn't (due to only working
against tapped vamps). I wouldn't go as high as half Ambush half Bum's
Rush, but 2:1 Bum's Rush:Ambush I think would be fairly reasonable.

: > to come by. It would have been a better design decision, I think, if
: > disciplineless Dodge were not so far inferior to Majesty, Earth Meld,
: > et al.

: And that has been my problem with it . . . just too easy to use.

Yeah. I think one of the larger mistakes the designers originally made
was that combat turned out to be a weaker strategy than they might have
expected. There are a whole lot of combat cards in Jyhad, but making
a combat deck that wins games is quite a bit more difficult than making
a non-combat deck that wins games. And many of the combat cards are
wallpaper or nearly wallpaper because they just don't work against the
readily available combat defenses. I think making Strike:Combat Ends
too good (and too easy to use) was part of the problem there.
